title: Protecting WordPress Contact Forms with AI
summary:

title: Building a browser GIF editor: the frame memory limit matters more than file size
summary:
I built VisualFormat, a free set of browser GIF tools. The files are processed locally, with no account required. One practical constraint shaped the implementation: a small GIF file can still be expensive to decode.

Start with decoded pixels

A 1,000 × 1,000 animation with 100 frames represents 100 million frame pixels. At four bytes per RGBA pixel, keeping a full decoded copy of every frame would already take roughly 400 MB, before working canvases and encoding buffers. The compressed download size does not describe that cost.

VisualFormat scans GIF blocks before allocating decoded frames. It checks dimensions, frame count and the total canvas pixels across the animation. The current GIF input limits are 20 MB, 500 frames, 4,096 pixels per dimension and 40 million total frame pixels. These are guardrails, not a guarantee that every device can process every accepted file.

title: Rewrite Rules for a Custom Post Type & Taxonomy Pattern
summary:
If you’ve ever built a Resources page for a custom WordPress theme, you’ve probably come accross bugs related or directly caused by the following pattern.

It’s not that clear what’s going on, but once you do figure it out you’ve probably implemented a bandaid approach that doesn’t quite give you the URL structure you originally planned. There are solution out there with alternative approaches, but I haven’t seen one that takes the following approach which will preserve the ideal URL pattern.

Post Type Rewrites With Zero Compromise

In an ideal world a Resources section of a custom WordPress powered website would have URL patterns like this:

  • /resources/ – Lists of all published resource posts using archive-resource.php as the theme template
  • /resources/{type}/ – List of all published resource posts of a specific type using taxonomy-resource_type.php as the theme template</

title: I built a repo where a first PR is one folder, and a 144-line validator reviews the format
summary:
I'm a beginner in open source. A few weeks ago a fairly big pull request of mine was merged into someone else's project, and the review taught me how much of a maintainer's time goes into checking things a machine could check.

So I tried to design a small repo where that part is automatic: skills-es, an open catalog of Spanish-language skills for Claude Code.

Disclosure: I built it with Claude's help and reviewed the result myself.

The idea

A "skill" is a folder with a SKILL.md file: reusable instructions an AI coding assistant can follow. Almost every catalog is in English, so this one is in Spanish.

The contribution unit is one folder:

skills/
my-skill/
SKILL.md
ejemplos/ejemplo.md

Adding a skill never touches code. That matters for people sending their first PR.

title: What I learned from building a relational database engine in C#
summary:
I’ve used Microsoft SQL Server for decades without ever seeing how it works inside. Sure, there’s ample documentation, but reading it isn’t the same thing as looking at the implementation code. Since the source is closed, I did the next best thing: I built my own relational database engine in C#, to face the same problems it must solve.

Today, my engine supports transactions, concurrency, and crash recovery. It also has a management tool. It can run both in-process and as a server, and I now rely on it in my daily work. For instance, my company’s invoicing goes through it.

I studied databases at university, and textbooks explain B-trees, SQL parsing, ACID principles, transactions, and recovery well. What they don’t show is how those pieces interact when something goes wrong at the worst possible moment. I quickly noticed that this was the thing left out of those books.
